parsed_answer.content: Java Message Service (JMS) is a Java Message Oriented Middleware (MOM) API that facilitates the enterprise-grade sending and receiving of messages between distributed applications. JMS basics encompass the core architecture required for asynchronous, loosely coupled communication, decoupling the message producer from the consumer via a common messaging broker. In high-throughput backend systems, synchronous HTTP or RPC calls can lead to cascading failures if a downstream service goes down. JMS solves this by introducing a durable message broker that buffers payloads, ensuring reliable delivery, load balancing across worker pools, and fault tolerance even during temporary network partitions or service outages.

At the heart of the JMS programming model are two primary messaging domains: Point-to-Point (Queues) and Publish-Subscribe (Topics). In the Point-to-Point domain, a message is addressed to a specific queue, and only one consumer from a pool of workers will successfully process that message, ensuring competing-consumer load balancing. Conversely, the Publish-Subscribe domain broadcasts messages to a topic, where multiple independent subscribers can register interest and receive their own independent copy of every published message, enabling event-driven architectures. Understanding these abstractions requires mastering administrative objects like ConnectionFactory, Destination, Connection, Session, MessageProducer, and MessageConsumer.

items: ConnectionFactory represents the configuration context used by a client to establish a socket-level connection to the JMS broker, handling credential negotiation and TCP pooling settings.

Session is a single-threaded context used for producing and consuming messages. It manages transactions, acknowledgments (CLIENT_ACKNOWLEDGE, AUTO_ACKNOWLEDGE, DUPS_OK_ACKNOWLEDGE), and local message factories.
Destinations encapsulate physical message stores on the broker: Queues for point-to-point routing and Topics for hierarchical or broadcast pub-sub message distribution.
Message lifecycle involves creation via session factories, setting optional headers (JMSCorrelationID, JMSExpiration, JMSPriority), and dispatching via producers.

parsed_answer.content: A common production trap in JMS is forgetting that Sessions are strictly single-threaded. Sharing a Session instance across multiple concurrent application threads will cause internal state corruption and undefined execution behaviors. Always instantiate a dedicated Session per thread or rely on connection/session pools provided by enterprise application servers or frameworks like Spring's DefaultJmsListenerContainer.
